A B S T R A C T
In the past decades, the microstructure and properties of tensile deformed high Mn–Al–C lightweight steels were
extensively studied due to their excellent combination of strength. ductility and low-density. However. the effects
of cold rolling were barely reported. This study systematically investigated the evolution of microstructure and
texture as well as mechanical properties during cold rolling of Fe–30Mn–11Al–1.2C (wt%) steel. The stacking
fault energy (SFE) of the steel was estimated as ~108 mJ/m<sup>2</sup>. With cold rolling, the yield strength of the steel
was significantly enhanced and exceeding 2.0 GPa after 90% rolling reduction, which is attributed to the gradual
refinement of the microstructure. Different deformation substructures were formed approximately in the
sequence of Taylor lattice, microbands, nano-twins, shear bands and dislocation cells. This means the dislocation
glide mode changes from planar to wavy glide with increasing rolling reduction. Among these structures, twining
is widely believed to be impossible by tensile deformation due to the high SFE. But it happened during cold
rolling with relatively low resolved shear stress, which may be attributed to the occurrence of short range order
(SRO) in austenitic matrix and local stress concentration. The rolling texture of the steel was weak and char
acterized by the transition from “copper-type” to “brass-type” after 50% rolling reduction. The dislocation planar
glide and deformation twining play an important role in texture evolution.

3.1. Mechanical properties
The mechanical properties of the present steel in the as-quenched
state as well as different cold rolling conditions are illustrated in
Fig. 1. The dark dash lines in Fig. 1(a) and (b) connect the necking point
of different samples. In the as-quenched state, the steel was character
ized by a low yield strength (YS) and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of
~570 MPa and ~ 830 MPa, respectively. But it exhibited a dramatic
uniform elongation (UE) of exceeding
which meant the excellent
work hardening capability. With the increase of cold rolling reduction,
the YS of material gradually increased and eventually reached
\mathrm { t o } \sim 2 . 0
GPa that is approximate 3.5 times of the as-quenched state. Simulta
neously, the materials lost its work hardening capability, resulting to the
decrease of the UE. Interestingly, the true stress of necking point was

3.2. Microstructure evolution
Fig. 2 shows the initial microstructure of the as-quenched materials
before cold rolling. The phase constituent was estimated as austenite
and κ’-carbides, and the nano-sized κ’-carbides were uniformly distrib
uted in the austenitic matrix. These κ’-carbides are formed via spinodal
decomposition during quenching, which is attributed to the high pre
cipitate kinetics caused by the high Al and C content
. The
microstructure contained a large amount of annealing twins, and the
grain size (including twins) is ~70 μm. In addition, the texture was
almost random distribution.
The optical micrographs of cold rolled microstructure are shown in
Fig. 3. According to the morphology features, the microstructure evo
lution could be subdivided into two stages: (I) In the first stage (10% to
50% rolling reduction), the microstructure was the typical low energy
dislocation structure (LEDS) of Taylor-lattice-type which was the result
of the planar dislocation glide (Fig. 3(a-c)). The different distance be
tween slip bands in different grains indicated that the deformation was
inhomogeneous and more pronounced in favorable orientation (Fig. 3
(a)). The characteristic of this stage is the gradual refinement of slip
bands space. (II) In the second stage (70% to 90% rolling reduction),
compared with stage I, a plenty of shear bands were observed, and the
grains were visibly elongated along the rolling direction (RD) (Fig. 3(c-
e)). The shear bands increased with cold rolling reduction and increas
ingly eroded the matrix to almost all of it. Therefore, the feature of this
stage is the gradual development of the shear bands.
Except the optical microscopy (OM), transmission electron micro
scopy (TEM) was also utilized to investigate the microstructure evolu
tion in detail (Fig. 4-6). It is clear that the Taylor-lattice consists of the
multiple slip bands (Fig. 4). The dislocations in the slip bands were
approximately parallel, and the dislocation pile-ups were found at the
intersections of the slip bands, as indicated by the green arrows in Fig. 4
(a). But the interaction of the non-coplanar slip bands was not strong to
completely impede the dislocation glide. Consequently, the dislocation
could across the intersection, making the slip bands across throughout
the whole grain. It is no doubt that the Taylor-lattice structure is
attributed to the planar dislocation glide [29], however, Sung-Dae Kim
etc. [30] found that the dislocation cross slip might occur at the inter
section, which could explain the weak interaction of the intersecting slip
bands. Up to 30% rolled reduction, there was no obvious variation on
structure except the gradual increase of the slip bands in Fig. 4(b). The
average slip band spacing of sample of 30% and 50% reduction are
measured as 231 nm and 64 nm, respectively.

reduction reached 50% as shown in Fig. 5. The single slip band was
hardly distinguishable. In addition, microbands were formed (indicated
by the pairs of green dashes line in Fig. 5(a)) with the average width of
166 nm. The different contrast between microbands and matrix reflects
that there is a misorientation among either side. Moreover, in some
grains, the intermittent linear structures in parallel arrangement were
detected, as shown in Fig. 5(b). According to the corresponding selected

Generally, there are two kinds of typical texture in FCC metal ma
terials, “copper-type texture” and “brass-type texture”. The former is
well understood which is favoured by the homogeneous deformation,
while the latter mechanism is not fully clear. In Cu–Mn alloys, the
texture transition from “Copper-type” to “Brass-type” was also observed,
and the transition took place earlier with the increase of Mn content
[40]. The authors attributed the transition to dislocation planar glide
because they did not observe deformation twins and sufficient shear
bands. Additionally, when deformation twining is activated (such as in
Cu–Zn alloy and TWIP steel etc.), the transition is interpreted by the
following orientation paths [20,21]. Twining occurs firstly in the grains
with Cu orientation, making orientation change to CuT. If the
morphology of twins is isolated, the twins will rotate to G orientation
around 〈110〉 axis by dislocation glide on the two coplanar systems,
(− 1− 11)[011] and (− 1− 10)[101], with the highest resolved shear
stress. Moreover, if the twins are located in the twin-matrix (T-M)
lamella, the situation will become more complex. Due to the spacing of
T-M lamella is very small, the dislocation is constrained to the common
{111} plane of twining plane, which leads to the abnormal rotation of
the twins and matrix, resulting in the higher Ф values. Eventually, the
twining plane (also the dislocation glide plane) is nearly parallel to the
rolling plane. The result of this phenomenon is that the resolved shear
stress decreases or even zero, and the deformation is unable to accom
modate by dislocation glide. Consequently, the micro shear bands are
generated by local strain concentration. These shear hands are reported
to consist of tiny grains, and the orientation of the grains is biased to
wards G and B. The G finally transformed to B through further dislo
cation slip.
In present work, the dislocation planar slip (as in Cu–Mn alloy)
dominates the deformation. In addition, deformation twins (as in Cu–Zn
alloy and TWIP steel etc.) are also detected (Fig. 3-6). And the twining

rolling reduction (Fig. 9(b)) and the slight strengthening of γ-fiber
texture (Fig. 9(c)). Specifically, the size of twins is nano-scale, forming
the fine T-M lamella structure (Fig. 5(d) and Fig. 6(a)). The shifts of Cu
and CuT (after symmetrical treatment) indicated by the red and blue
arrows in Fig. 9(b) are consistent with the latent hardening process.
Furthermore, the microshear bands generated by the local strain con
centration are extensively observed, with accompanying by the rapid
increase of the G component (Fig. 3(c-e) and Fig. 6(b)). In conclusion,
above two mechanisms may be both contributed to the transition from
“Copper-type texture” to “Brass-type texture”.
5. Conclusions
The effect of cold rolling on the microstructure, texture and me
chanical properties of Fe–30Mn–11Al–1.2C austenitic low-density steel
is investigated. Major conclusions are summarized as follows:
1. With the increasing of cold rolling reduction, the yield strength is
significantly enhanced up to ~2.0 GPa and the elongation decreases.
The strengthening mechanism of the present steel with low rolling
reduction of 10–30% is the refinement of the slip bands spacing. At
higher reductions of 50–90%, the Hall-Petch effect induced by
microbands, twins, dislocation tangles and grain refinement plays an
important role in enhancing strength.
2. The deformation substructure evolution during cold rolling approx
imately follows the sequence of Taylor lattice, microbands, twins,
shear bands and dislocation tangles. Among them, the deformation
twins are activated with the stress much lower than the critical stress,
which may due to the short range order phase and the local stress
concentration.
3. The intensity of the whole texture is relative weak, which may due to
the planar dislocation glide. A “copper-type texture” is formed at
50% rolling reduction while it gradually transformed to “brass-type
texture” with further rolling. The transition is attributed both to the
dislocation planar glide and deformation twins.

with Cu orientation, making orientation change to CuT. If the
morphology of twins is isolated, the twins will rotate to G orientation
around 〈110〉 axis by dislocation glide on the two coplanar systems,
(− 1− 11)[011] and (− 1− 10)[101], with the highest resolved shear
stress. Moreover, if the twins are located in the twin-matrix (T-M)
lamella, the situation will become more complex. Due to the spacing of
T-M lamella is very small, the dislocation is constrained to the common
{111} plane of twining plane, which leads to the abnormal rotation of
the twins and matrix, resulting in the higher Ф values. Eventually, the
twining plane (also the dislocation glide plane) is nearly parallel to the
rolling plane. The result of this phenomenon is that the resolved shear
stress decreases or even zero, and the deformation is unable to accom
modate by dislocation glide. Consequently, the micro shear bands are
generated by local strain concentration. These shear hands are reported
to consist of tiny grains, and the orientation of the grains is biased to
wards G and B. The G finally transformed to B through further dislo
cation slip.
In present work, the dislocation planar slip (as in Cu–Mn alloy)
dominates the deformation. In addition, deformation twins (as in Cu–Zn
alloy and TWIP steel etc.) are also detected (Fig. 3-6). And the twining
can also be indirectly reflected by the development of CuT after 50%
rolling reduction (Fig. 9(b)) and the slight strengthening of γ-fiber
texture (Fig. 9(c)). Specifically, the size of twins is nano-scale, forming
the fine T-M lamella structure (Fig. 5(d) and Fig. 6(a)). The shifts of Cu
and CuT (after symmetrical treatment) indicated by the red and blue
arrows in Fig. 9(b) are consistent with the latent hardening process.
Furthermore, the microshear bands generated by the local strain con
centration are extensively observed, with accompanying by the rapid
increase of the G component (Fig. 3(c-e) and Fig. 6(b)). In conclusion,
above two mechanisms may be both contributed to the transition from
“Copper-type texture” to “Brass-type texture”.
5. Conclusions
The effect of cold rolling on the microstructure, texture and me
chanical properties of Fe–30Mn–11Al–1.2C austenitic low-density steel
is investigated. Major conclusions are summarized as follows:
1. With the increasing of cold rolling reduction, the yield strength is
significantly enhanced up to ~2.0 GPa and the elongation decreases.
The strengthening mechanism of the present steel with low rolling
reduction of 10–30% is the refinement of the slip bands spacing. At
higher reductions of 50–90%, the Hall-Petch effect induced by
microbands, twins, dislocation tangles and grain refinement plays an
important role in enhancing strength.
2. The deformation substructure evolution during cold rolling approx
imately follows the sequence of Taylor lattice, microbands, twins,
shear bands and dislocation tangles. Among them, the deformation
twins are activated with the stress much lower than the critical stress,
which may due to the short range order phase and the local stress
concentration.
3. The intensity of the whole texture is relative weak, which may due to
the planar dislocation glide. A “copper-type texture” is formed at
50% rolling reduction while it gradually transformed to “brass-type
texture” with further rolling. The transition is attributed both to the
dislocation planar glide and deformation twins.
